title: The Prince and the Pebble
hookLine: a prince sets a trap, a baby on his lap gives the answer, and a neighbor's poem about seasons
carry: right speech: true, helpful, then the right time
tomorrow: what changes when you listen without loading your reply?

lines: A BABY ON THE PRINCE'S LAP.
cards: A friend's bad haircut, pointed out the night before her school photo. A brother's grade, announced at the dinner table. An apology, ready to go, while the person who needs it is asleep on the couch.
True, all three. So is a true thing, said at the wrong moment, still right speech? A prince once tried to trap the Buddha with that question, and a baby sitting on the prince's lap gave the answer.

teach.b: Prince Abhaya came with a trick question: would you ever say something unwelcome? Say yes, and you're as harsh as anyone. Say no, and explain the hard things you've said.
The Buddha looked at the baby on Abhaya's lap.

teach.h: A PEBBLE IN THE BABY'S MOUTH.
teach.b: If your child put a pebble in his mouth, what would you do? I'd get it out, the prince said, even if it drew a little blood. Because I love him.
So the Buddha sorted words three ways: true or not, helpful or not, welcome or not. Untrue, he doesn't say. True but unhelpful, he doesn't say.
True and helpful, welcome or not, he knows the right time to say it. Timing is the last check, after truth and help. Now a neighbor.
In Ecclesiastes, a book Jews and Christians share, comes a poem of seasons.

teach.h: A TIME TO SPEAK, IN ECCLESIASTES.
teach.b: In the King James words: "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven," and among them, "a time to keep silence, and a time to speak."
Shared ground: both see that silence and speech each have their hour.

One honest difference: in Ecclesiastes the times are set under heaven, and a few verses on, God "hath made every thing beautiful in his time." The Buddha's version is a judgment the speaker makes, after two other checks.
Neither text says the hard words go unsaid forever. Both say: wait for the hour, then speak.

how: Buddhist teachers often teach right speech with MN 58's checks (true, beneficial, and the right time); Jews and Christians read the seasons poem of Ecclesiastes 3, which is sometimes read at weddings and funerals.

o: an auspicious hour chosen by the stars
a rule to speak only when people want to hear it
the moment true, helpful words can be heard

games.q: the prince, the pebble and a poem — tap the pairs.
p: taken out of the baby's mouth, out of love
said at the right time, welcome or not
a time to keep silence, and a time to speak

s: in MN 58, the Buddha never says anything people don't want to hear
true and helpful words, even unwelcome ones, he says at the right time, like taking a pebble from a baby's mouth.
in MN 58, timing comes after two checks: is it true, is it helpful
untrue or unhelpful words he doesn't say at all; timing is the last check.
Ecclesiastes says there is a time to keep silence and a time to speak
Ecclesiastes 3:7, in the poem of seasons Jews and Christians share.

games.q: your best friend's sketch for the art show has a mistake, and she doesn't see it. it's true and it would help. the show is in a week. what does MN 58 point to?
o: say nothing; unwelcome words aren't right speech.
tell her right now, in front of the group, since it's true.
tell her, at a moment she can hear it and still fix it.
games.why: true and helpful words, even unwelcome, the Buddha says at the right time. here the right time is soon, in private, while she can still fix it.

practice: Bring to mind one true thing you need to say to someone close. Ask it the three questions slowly: is it true, is it helpful, and when could they actually hear it?
Settle on the moment, maybe tomorrow at breakfast, maybe a walk this weekend, and let the words wait there, ready, until it comes.

wordCard.voice: The right time: the last check on true, helpful words. In Pali, kala, time; in MN 58 the Buddha knows the time to speak.

orig.note: Pali: time, the right moment; in MN 58 the Buddha knows the time to speak.

carryVoice: Keep this one close: right speech is true, then helpful, then said at the right time. Two of four, on speech at home.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 58 (Abhayarajakumara Sutta: Prince Abhaya's two-horned question; the infant with a stick or pebble in its mouth; speech sorted by true, beneficial and welcome, and the Tathagata knowing the time to speak)
